Stirreth
STIR-eth
v. (3rd pers. sing.)
The third-person singular present of stir, from Saxon styrian, to move, to agitate. Webster 1828: moveth; agitateth; exciteth. Scripture uses it of an eagle rousing her young, of a proud heart raising strife, and of hell itself roused to meet a fallen king.

Biblical Definition

Stirreth is a word of rousing, and Scripture applies it to God’s care, to man’s pride, and to the grave. The tenderest use is God’s own picture of how He taught Israel: As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings (Deuteronomy 32:11). The nest is broken up deliberately so that the eaglets will fly, and the same wings that disturb them catch them. That is the shape of God’s hard providences toward His people: the comfortable place is unsettled by the One who intends to carry them. Proverbs uses the word twice of what a bad heart produces: Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins (Proverbs 10:12), and He that is of a proud heart stirreth up strife: but he that putteth his trust in the LORD shall be made fat (Proverbs 28:25). In both, strife is not an accident of circumstance but the output of a settled disposition. And Isaiah gives the word its most terrible use, as the grave rouses its inhabitants to greet the king of Babylon: Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, even all the chief ones of the earth (Isaiah 14:9).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 gives STIRRETH as the third person singular of STIR: to move; to agitate; to bring into debate or action; to incite, instigate, or excite, as to stir up strife or to stir up the mind.

STIRRETH — the third person singular, present tense, of the verb STIR.

STIR, v.t. — To move; to change place in any manner; to agitate what is at rest.

To incite to action; to instigate; to prompt; as, to stir up a people to rebellion.

To excite or raise; as, to stir up strife, contention, or the affections.

From Saxon styrian, to move — connected with storm and with stern in its older sense of stirring or violent.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 32:11 — "As an eagle stirreth up her nest, fluttereth over her young, spreadeth abroad her wings, taketh them, beareth them on her wings:"

Proverbs 10:12 — "Hatred stirreth up strifes: but love covereth all sins."

Proverbs 28:25 — "He that is of a proud heart stirreth up strife: but he that putteth his trust in the LORD shall be made fat."

Isaiah 14:9 — "Hell from beneath is moved for thee to meet thee at thy coming: it stirreth up the dead for thee, even all the chief ones of the earth; it hath raised up from their thrones all the kings of the nations."

Modern Corruption

Proverbs traces strife to a proud heart in the man who raises it, and the modern habit of explaining conflict entirely by circumstance, systems, or the other party’s behaviour removes the one cause Scripture actually names.

expand to see more

Proverbs 10:12 and 28:25 both put the cause inside the man: hatred stirs up strifes; a proud heart stirs up strife. James asks the same question and gives the same answer — From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members? (James 4:1). Against that stands the now-dominant habit of accounting for conflict by structures, personality types, communication styles, or the wounds a person carries, all of which may be genuinely present and none of which is the biblical diagnosis. The practical consequence is enormous: if strife proceeds from pride in me, then the first move in every quarrel is repentance, and I can make it without waiting for the other party. If strife proceeds from circumstance, I must wait for the circumstance to change, and I usually wait for ever.

Deuteronomy 32:11 corrects a corruption of the opposite kind — the assumption that a settled, comfortable life is the mark of God’s favour. The eagle deliberately breaks up the nest. The disturbance is not the withdrawal of care but its exercise, and the wings that unsettle are the wings that bear. Read against Isaiah 14:9, where hell itself is stirred up to receive a man who exalted himself, the two uses frame the alternative plainly: God stirs His people out of comfort in order to carry them, and the proud man stirs up strife until the grave stirs to meet him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ur (H5782), to rouse, to awake, to stir up; garah (H1624), to stir up strife, to contend; Greek diegeiro (G1326), to arouse thoroughly; anazopureo (G329), to stir into flame.

expand to see more

Hebrew ur (H5782) — to rouse, to awake; the eagle stirring her nest (Deuteronomy 32:11) and hell stirring the dead (Isaiah 14:9).

Hebrew garah (H1624) — to stir up, to contend, to meddle; hatred stirreth up strifes (Proverbs 10:12).

Hebrew madon (H4066) — strife, contention; the noun that garah produces in Proverbs 28:25.

Greek diegeiro (G1326) — to arouse completely; Peter stirs up his readers by putting you in remembrance (2 Peter 1:13).

Greek anazopureo (G329) — to rekindle, to fan into flame; stir up the gift of God, which is in thee (2 Timothy 1:6).

Usage

"As an eagle stirreth up her nest (Deuteronomy 32:11) — the nest broken up by the One who means to carry them."

"Hatred stirreth up strifes (Proverbs 10:12) — conflict traced to a disposition, not a circumstance."

"It stirreth up the dead for thee (Isaiah 14:9) — the grave rousing to meet a fallen king."
